To further account for the heterogeneous reasoning distributions across knowledge states, we introduce a quadrant-adaptive distillation objective: reverse KL for concentrated integration, forward KL for diverse refusal, and Pareto-optimal bidirectional KL for asymmetric quadrants requiring both precision and coverage. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that KbSD consistently improves both task accuracy and hallucination mitigation over strong baselines, with the largest gains appearing in the challenging quadrants where sparse rewards are least informative.

summary.takeaway: KbSD introduces a quadrant-adaptive self-distillation framework that provides dense token-level supervision and tailored KL divergence objectives to improve knowledge boundary calibration in agentic search.
summary.problem: Existing reinforcement learning methods for agentic search suffer from sparse binary rewards that inadequately guide the reasoning process for calibrated decisions across heterogeneous knowledge states.
summary.method: KbSD constructs a hint-augmented teacher model identical to the student that receives explicit knowledge boundary signals to generate dense reasoning demonstrations and applies quadrant-adaptive KL objectives for optimized distillation.
summary.evidence: Experiments on nine benchmarks with Qwen2.5 models show KbSD consistently reduces unreliability rates and improves task accuracy and hallucination mitigation compared to strong baselines including KbPO and RL-based agents.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis on computational overhead or generalization beyond the tested benchmarks and model scales.
summary.why_for_you: KbSD’s approach to dense process-level supervision and quadrant-specific optimization offers a novel solution to reward sparsity and heterogeneous reasoning distributions in trustworthy agentic LLMs.

signals.text: KbSD achieves an absolute reduction of approximately 17 points in unreliability rate on Qwen2.5-3B and 7B models compared to KbPO, demonstrating improved behavioral calibration across knowledge boundary quadrants.

The quadrant-adaptive distillation objective applies reverse KL divergence for concentrated integration in Quadrant 1, forward KL for diverse refusal in Quadrant 3, and bidirectional KL for asymmetric quadrants 2 and 4, enabling tailored optimization per knowledge state.

Ablation studies show that removing the distillation loss or replacing quadrant-adaptive KL with fixed KL variants degrades performance, confirming the necessity of dense supervision and adaptive divergence measures for effective calibration.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of reward sparsity in agentic search systems where large language models must decide when to trust internal parametric memory, rely on retrieved evidence, or abstain from answering. Traditional binary rewards provide insufficient guidance on the intermediate reasoning steps necessary for calibrated decisions across four knowledge boundary quadrants defined by internal certainty and retrieval quality. KbSD proposes a self-distillation framework that constructs a hint-augmented teacher model receiving explicit knowledge boundary signals to generate dense token-level supervision. This dense supervision complements sparse outcome-level rewards and is optimized with quadrant-adaptive KL divergence objectives tailored to the heterogeneous reasoning distributions of each quadrant. Experiments on nine diverse benchmarks using Qwen2.5 models demonstrate that KbSD consistently lowers unreliability rates and improves task accuracy and hallucination mitigation compared to strong baselines, especially in challenging quadrants where sparse rewards are least informative. Ablations validate the importance of dense supervision and adaptive KL objectives, establishing KbSD as an effective method for behavioral calibration in agentic search.

methodology.title: Hint-Augmented Teacher Construction
methodology.detail: KbSD builds a teacher model architecturally identical to the student that receives explicit knowledge boundary signals including parametric certainty, retrieval quality, and ground-truth answers. This teacher generates calibrated reasoning demonstrations providing dense token-level supervision to the student without requiring a larger external model.

methodology.title: Quadrant-Adaptive Distillation Objective
methodology.detail: The distillation loss applies different KL divergence measures per knowledge quadrant: reverse KL for concentrated, unimodal integration in Quadrant 1; forward KL for diverse refusal behavior in Quadrant 3; and Pareto-optimal bidirectional KL for asymmetric quadrants 2 and 4 requiring both precision and coverage.

methodology.title: Integration of Dense Supervision and Sparse Rewards
methodology.detail: KbSD combines dense token-level supervision from the teacher with sparse outcome-level rewards to guide the agent’s reasoning process and behavior selection during multi-turn agentic search, addressing reward sparsity at the process level.

methodology.title: Training Setup and Optimization
methodology.detail: Training uses the VERL framework with GRPO optimizer, generating multiple rollouts per query. Hyperparameters include learning rate 1e-6, KL coefficient 0.001, process reward weight 0.2, and distillation weight 0.1. Knowledge boundary thresholds are set to 0.5 and 0.6 for parametric certainty and retrieval quality.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models for the knowledge boundary calibration mechanism but describes the quadrant taxonomy and adaptive KL objectives conceptually.

experiments.title: Datasets and Benchmarks
experiments.detail: Training data is synthesized from HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA. Evaluation spans nine benchmarks across multi-hop QA, open-domain QA, and agentic reasoning categories, including HotpotQA, TriviaQA, NQ, GAIA, and FRAMES.

experiments.title: Models and Retrieval
experiments.detail: Experiments use Qwen2.5 backbone models at 3B and 7B parameter scales. Retrieval is performed with the E5 dense retriever over the 2018 Wikipedia dump, retrieving top-3 passages per query.

experiments.title: Baselines and Metrics
experiments.detail: Comparisons include standard RAG methods (Naive RAG, FS-RAG, FLARE), agentic RAG methods (ReAct, IRCoT, Self-RAG, CRAG), and RL-based agents (Search-R1, ARPO, AEPO, MEM1, KbPO). Metrics are F1 for task utility and unreliability rate (1 - (F1 + refusal rate)) for unsafe behaviors.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Ablations on Qwen2.5-3B analyze the impact of removing distillation loss and replacing quadrant-adaptive KL with fixed KL variants, demonstrating performance degradation and validating the design choices.

findings.title: Improved Reliability Across Scales
findings.detail: KbSD reduces unreliability rate from 64.32 to 47.60 on Qwen2.5-3B and from 57.99 to 41.18 on Qwen2.5-7B compared to KbPO, showing consistent gains with larger model capacity.

findings.title: Superior Calibration on Challenging Quadrants
findings.detail: KbSD achieves the largest performance improvements on benchmarks requiring precise knowledge boundary calibration, such as TriviaQA and NQ, outperforming Search-R1 and AEPO.

findings.title: Necessity of Dense Supervision
findings.detail: Removing the distillation loss leads to performance drops across all benchmarks, confirming that dense token-level supervision is essential for guiding the reasoning process.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Quadrant-Adaptive KL
findings.detail: Replacing quadrant-adaptive KL with fixed forward or reverse KL harms performance, especially on benchmarks requiring diverse refusal or concentrated integration, validating the adaptive divergence approach.

findings.title: Balanced Quadrant Rebalancing
findings.detail: Proper calibration between the four quadrants reduces unreliability rates, avoiding hallucination from over-rewarding internal answers and loss of helpfulness from over-rewarding refusal.

contributions: Proposed KbSD, a self-distillation framework with a hint-augmented teacher for dense token-level supervision in agentic search.
Introduced a quadrant-adaptive KL divergence objective tailored to heterogeneous reasoning distributions across knowledge boundary quadrants.
Demonstrated consistent improvements in task accuracy and hallucination mitigation over strong baselines on nine diverse benchmarks.
Validated the necessity of dense supervision and adaptive divergence through comprehensive ablation studies.
limitations: Lack of analysis on computational cost and efficiency of the self-distillation framework.
No exploration of generalization to other model architectures beyond Qwen2.5 or to retrieval systems beyond E5.
Absence of formal mechanistic or theoretical modeling of the knowledge boundary calibration process.
Limited discussion on the impact of hyperparameter sensitivity or robustness across different task domains.
open_questions: How does KbSD scale computationally and perform in real-time or resource-constrained agentic search applications?
Can the quadrant-adaptive distillation approach generalize to other LLM architectures or retrieval paradigms?
What are the theoretical guarantees or limitations of using KL divergence variants for heterogeneous reasoning distributions?
How can the framework be extended to incorporate richer knowledge boundary signals or multi-modal evidence?

papers.title: Can Agents Generalize to the Open World? Unveiling the Fragility of Static Training in Tool Use
papers.abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents demonstrate proficiency in static benchmarks, their deployment in real-world scenarios is hindered by the dynamic nature of user queries, tool sets, and interaction dynamics. To address this generalization gap, we formalize OpenAgent (Tool-Use Agent in Open-World), a problem setting characterized by distributional shifts across query, action, observation, and domain dimensions. To systematically diagnose its impact, we construct a controlled sandbox environment where we define fine-grained environmental shifts across a four-tier hierarchy, Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization, and conduct a comprehensive series of experiments. Our analysis yields a series of key insights, demonstrating that agents trained via both Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT) and Reinforcement Learning suffer from varying degrees of performance degradation when confronting open environmental shifts. Building on these insights, we propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning, a disturbance-based intervention strategy for SFT that lays the foundation for enhancing agent robustness and utility in realistic environments. Our code will be released at: https://github. com/LAMDA-NeSy/OpenAgent.

summary.takeaway: LLM agents trained via Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning exhibit significant performance degradation under open-world distributional shifts, which can be partially mitigated by Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning.
summary.problem: Current LLM agents trained under static assumptions fail to generalize effectively to dynamic, open-world tool-use environments characterized by shifts in queries, tools, interactions, and domains.
summary.method: The authors formalize the OpenAgent problem setting, construct a controlled sandbox environment with a four-tier hierarchy of environmental shifts, and propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning to improve robustness.
summary.evidence: Comprehensive experiments in the sandbox environment demonstrate that both SFT and RL agents suffer from distinct failure modes and performance drops under open-world shifts, with PAFT improving SFT robustness.
summary.limitations: The study focuses on a synthetic sandbox environment and does not provide evidence of PAFT’s effectiveness in fully real-world, large-scale deployments or across diverse tool-use domains.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a rigorous framework and empirical insights into the generalization challenges of tool-using LLM agents, offering a novel fine-tuning strategy relevant for enhancing trustworthy and efficient adversarial training.

signals.text: The study identifies symbolic anchoring as a critical failure mode in Supervised Fine-Tuning agents, causing brittle reliance on shallow patterns that degrade performance under tool schema shifts.

Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT) injects controlled observation anomalies and symbolic noise during training to decouple models from memorization and enhance robustness to open-world perturbations.

Experimental results show that Reinforcement Learning agents maintain higher active exploration scores (>0.86 AES) under tool redirection and value redirection shifts, whereas SFT agents’ scores collapse near zero.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical gap in generalization of LLM agents trained under static assumptions when deployed in dynamic, open-world environments. The authors formalize the OpenAgent setting, capturing distributional shifts across user queries, tool sets, interaction dynamics, and task domains. To systematically analyze these shifts, they design a controlled sandbox environment with a four-tier hierarchy—Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization—allowing precise injection of perturbations. Through extensive experiments comparing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents, the study reveals distinct failure modes: SFT agents suffer from symbolic anchoring and trajectory overfitting, while RL agents exhibit boundary blindness due to reward structure biases. To mitigate these issues, the authors propose Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT), a data-centric approach that introduces controlled noise during training to improve robustness. Empirical evidence demonstrates PAFT’s effectiveness in restoring generalization capabilities, highlighting the fragility of static training and the necessity of disturbance-based interventions for real-world tool-use agent deployment.

methodology.title: OpenAgent Formalization
methodology.detail: The agent is modeled as a sequential decision-making process M = ⟨Q, A, O, π⟩, where Q is user queries, A is tool action space, O is observation space, and π is the policy. The OpenAgent setting characterizes distributional shifts across queries (∆Q), actions (∆A), observations (∆O), and domains (∆D), focusing on generalization when test distributions diverge from training.

methodology.title: Controlled Sandbox Environment
methodology.detail: A synthetic sandbox environment is constructed to isolate and systematically inject environmental shifts across four tiers: Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization. This controlled setup avoids transient noise from real-world APIs, enabling precise evaluation of agent robustness to open-world perturbations.

methodology.title: Training Paradigms and Baselines
methodology.detail: The study compares full-parameter Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Reinforcement Learning (RL) with the GRPO framework. Both models are trained to convergence under comparable computational budgets in the closed environment to establish baselines.

methodology.title: Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT)
methodology.detail: PAFT is a disturbance-based intervention for SFT that injects controlled observation anomalies and symbolic noise into training trajectories. This approach aims to prevent shallow pattern memorization and improve generalization by forcing the model to learn robust representations under noisy conditions.

mechanism.title: Failure Modes in Training Paradigms
mechanism.detail: SFT agents exhibit symbolic anchoring, where they overfit to specific tool invocation patterns, leading to brittle performance under schema shifts. RL agents, while better at semantic grounding, suffer from boundary blindness caused by teleological biases in reward structures, limiting their adaptability to novel tool configurations.

experiments.title: Evaluation of Instruction Robustness (∆Q)
experiments.detail: Agents are tested on their ability to handle instruction blurring and information redundancy, simulating real-world user input variability. The evaluation uses a dataset of 6,050 training and 880 evaluation samples with strict separation to prevent pattern leakage.

experiments.title: Tiered Environmental Shift Experiments
experiments.detail: Experiments inject perturbations across Perception, Interaction, Reasoning, and Internalization tiers in the sandbox. Metrics include task success rates and Active Exploration Scores (AES) to quantify agent adaptability under null returns, error returns, tool redirection, and value redirection.

experiments.title: Comparison of SFT and RL Agents
experiments.detail: Both paradigms are trained on the same backbone and evaluated under identical conditions. RL agents maintain near-perfect AES (>0.86) under tool redirection shifts, whereas SFT agents’ AES collapse near zero, indicating distinct robustness profiles.

experiments.title: PAFT Intervention Evaluation
experiments.detail: PAFT is applied to SFT agents by augmenting training data with controlled noise. Results show improved robustness and utility in open environments, partially restoring generalization lost due to symbolic anchoring.

findings.title: Performance Degradation under Open-World Shifts
findings.detail: Both SFT and RL agents experience significant performance drops when exposed to distributional shifts in queries, tools, interactions, and domains, confirming the fragility of static training assumptions.

findings.title: Distinct Failure Modes for SFT and RL
findings.detail: SFT agents suffer from trajectory overfitting and symbolic anchoring, leading to brittle tool invocation, while RL agents show boundary blindness due to reward teleology, limiting their semantic adaptability.

findings.title: RL Agents’ Superior Active Exploration
findings.detail: Under tool redirection and value redirection perturbations, RL agents maintain high Active Exploration Scores (>0.86), indicating better adaptability compared to SFT agents whose scores collapse near zero.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning
findings.detail: PAFT improves SFT agents’ robustness by injecting controlled noise during training, mitigating symbolic anchoring and enhancing generalization to open-world shifts.

contributions: Formalization of the OpenAgent problem setting capturing multi-dimensional distributional shifts in tool-use environments.
Development of a controlled sandbox environment with a four-tier hierarchy for systematic evaluation of agent robustness.
Identification of critical failure modes: symbolic anchoring in SFT and boundary blindness in RL.
Proposal of Perturbation-Augmented Fine-Tuning (PAFT) as a data-centric method to enhance SFT robustness.
Comprehensive empirical analysis comparing SFT and RL paradigms under open-world perturbations.
limitations: Evaluation is limited to a synthetic sandbox environment, which may not fully capture complexities of real-world tool-use scenarios.
PAFT’s effectiveness is demonstrated only on SFT agents and not extended to RL or hybrid paradigms.
The study does not explore scalability of PAFT to larger models or diverse tool sets beyond the tested tasks.
No direct evidence is provided on long-term deployment stability or user-centric metrics in open environments.
open_questions: How can PAFT or similar disturbance-based methods be integrated with RL or hybrid training paradigms to improve robustness?
What are the scalability limits of PAFT when applied to larger LLMs and more complex, heterogeneous tool ecosystems?
Can the four-tier hierarchy of environmental shifts be extended or refined to better model real-world deployment dynamics?
How do these findings translate to real-world APIs and user interactions with noisy, evolving tool sets?

papers.title: MOPD: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Capability Integration in LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) rely on reinforcement learning during post-training to push specific capabilities, yet integrating multiple capabilities into one model remains hard. Existing methods, such as Off-Policy Finetune and Mix-RL, are either inefficient or lose performance. In this work, we propose Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), a post-training paradigm for combining the capabilities of multiple domain RL teachers: we first run per-domain specialised RL to obtain a set of domain teachers, then distill these teachers into the student on its own rollouts. This eliminates exposure bias and provides a dense optimization signal. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MOPD outperforms Mix-RL, Cascade RL, Off-Policy Finetune, and Param-Merge baselines, inheriting nearly all of each teacher's capability. MOPD also enables parallel, independent development of domain teachers, removing the cross-domain coupling typical of multi-domain post-training. MOPD has been deployed in the post-training of MiMo-V2-Flash, an industrial-scale frontier model, demonstrating its practical value for capability integration in frontier-scale LLMs.

summary.takeaway: MOPD integrates multiple domain-specific RL teachers into a single LLM via on-policy distillation, achieving superior multi-domain capability without exposure bias or training instability.
summary.problem: Existing multi-capability integration methods for LLM post-training either suffer from inefficiency, exposure bias, instability, or performance degradation.
summary.method: MOPD first trains specialized RL teachers per domain, then distills their policies into a student model on the student's own rollouts using a reverse KL loss with per-prompt teacher dispatch.
summary.evidence: On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MOPD outperforms Mix-RL, Cascade RL, Off-Policy Finetune, and Param-Merge baselines by 5.5 normalized score points, closing 91–95% of the teacher-student performance gap across domains.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed ablations on the impact of teacher quality variance or the scalability limits of MOPD to more than three domains.
summary.why_for_you: MOPD offers a scalable, stable, and efficient on-policy distillation framework for integrating multiple RL-trained capabilities into a single LLM, directly addressing exposure bias and cross-domain interference.

signals.text: MOPD achieves dense optimization by distilling token-level log-probabilities from multiple frozen domain teachers on the student's own rollout distribution, enabling the student to inherit nearly all capabilities of each teacher.
The method uses a per-token reverse KL loss with two implementations: a policy-gradient form with clipped advantages and a top-k distillation loss that reduces variance and infrastructure overhead.
MOPD eliminates exposure bias by training on the student’s own rollout distribution rather than off-policy teacher rollouts, avoiding the canonical exposure bias seen in Off-Policy Finetune.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of integrating multiple domain-specific capabilities into a single large language model (LLM) during post-training, a problem where existing methods like Mix-RL, Cascade RL, Off-Policy Finetune, and Param-Merge trade off efficiency, stability, and performance. MOPD proposes a novel on-policy distillation paradigm that first trains specialized RL teachers independently per domain, then distills their policies into a student model by routing each prompt to the corresponding teacher and optimizing a reverse KL loss on the student's own rollouts. This approach provides dense token-level supervision, eliminates exposure bias, and avoids unstable weight-space fusion. Empirical results on Qwen3-30B-A3B across math, instruction following, and software engineering domains demonstrate that MOPD surpasses all baselines by a significant margin, closing most of the gap between the student and specialized teachers. The method also supports parallel teacher development and multi-round student-teacher evolution, making it practical for industrial-scale LLM post-training.

methodology.title: Stage 1: Specialized RL Teacher Training
methodology.detail: Train domain-specific RL teachers independently using specialized pipelines per domain (e.g., verifiable-answer RL for math, agent-style RL for software engineering). Each teacher is frozen after training.

methodology.title: Stage 2: Student Rollout Generation
methodology.detail: The student model generates rollouts by sampling from its own policy distribution, ensuring on-policy data collection that matches the student’s behavior and eliminates exposure bias.

methodology.title: Stage 3: On-Policy Distillation with Per-Prompt Teacher Dispatch
methodology.detail: Each student rollout prompt is routed to the corresponding frozen domain teacher, which provides token-level log-probabilities. The student is optimized via a reverse KL loss between its policy and the dispatched teacher’s policy.

methodology.title: Loss Implementations
methodology.detail: Two loss variants are used: (1) a policy-gradient form with clipped per-token advantages derived from log-probability differences, compatible with PPO/GRPO frameworks; (2) a top-k distillation loss that uses the teacher’s top-k tokens to reduce variance and infrastructure load.

methodology.title: Infrastructure Optimization
methodology.detail: Teacher prefill computations are decoupled from the RL training loop to reduce latency and complexity, enabling efficient per-token log-probability retrieval during distillation.

mechanism.title: On-Policy Distillation via Reverse KL Loss
mechanism.detail: The student policy π_θ is optimized to minimize the reverse KL divergence to the dispatched teacher policy π_φd on the student’s own rollout distribution, expressed as L_rev-KL = E_{x,y~π_θ}[∑_t π_φd(y_t) log(π_θ(y_t))], ensuring dense token-level supervision and stable policy updates.

mechanism.title: Advantage Clipping for Stability
mechanism.detail: The per-token advantage Â_MOPD,t = clip(log π_φd(y_t) - log π_θ(y_t), -A_max, +A_max) is clipped on both sides to prevent large gradient variance and stabilize training within policy-gradient frameworks.

mechanism.title: Top-k Token Distillation Correction
mechanism.detail: The top-k distillation loss includes an additional term π_φd(v) - π_θ(v) beyond the standard reverse KL to correct bias from truncating the teacher’s distribution to top-k tokens, ensuring the loss is minimized when the student matches the teacher on these tokens.

experiments.title: Capability Integration on Qwen3-30B-A3B
experiments.detail: Evaluated on three domains: Math (AIME25, AIME26), Instruction Following (IFBench, IFEval), and Software Engineering (SWE-bench Verified). Baselines include Mix-RL, Cascade RL, Off-Policy Finetune, and Param-Merge. Metrics are per-domain accuracy and a normalized score that scales performance relative to the Stage-1 student and Stage-2 specialist teachers.

experiments.title: Baseline Comparisons
experiments.detail: MOPD outperforms all baselines by 5.5 normalized score points, closing 91–95% of the gap between the Stage-1 student and specialized RL teachers, demonstrating superior multi-domain capability integration.

experiments.title: Loss Variant Ablations
experiments.detail: Both policy-gradient and top-k loss implementations perform comparably, validating the flexibility of MOPD’s distillation approach.

experiments.title: Industrial Deployment
experiments.detail: MOPD was deployed in the post-training of MiMo-V2-Flash, an industrial-scale frontier LLM, where it matched or exceeded teacher performance on most benchmarks, demonstrating practical scalability.

findings.title: Superior Integration Performance
findings.detail: MOPD leads all baselines on Qwen3-30B-A3B with a normalized score improvement of 5.5 points, effectively inheriting nearly all capabilities of each domain teacher.

findings.title: Exposure Bias Elimination
findings.detail: Training on the student’s own rollouts removes exposure bias inherent in off-policy finetuning, contributing to stable and effective capability integration.

findings.title: Stable and Parallelizable Training
findings.detail: Policy-space integration via per-prompt routing avoids unstable weight-space fusion and enables parallel, independent teacher development.

findings.title: Loss Implementation Flexibility
findings.detail: Both policy-gradient and top-k distillation loss forms yield comparable results, offering trade-offs between variance and infrastructure complexity.

findings.title: Multi-Round Student-Teacher Evolution
findings.detail: The pipeline supports iterative improvement cycles between student and teachers, enhancing capability integration over multiple rounds.

contributions: Proposed MOPD, a novel multi-teacher on-policy distillation paradigm for LLM capability integration.
Demonstrated elimination of exposure bias by training on student rollouts with per-prompt teacher dispatch.
Developed two efficient loss implementations (policy-gradient and top-k) for stable distillation.
Empirically validated MOPD’s superiority over four strong baselines on a large-scale LLM across three diverse domains.
Showcased practical deployment of MOPD in industrial-scale LLM post-training with MiMo-V2-Flash.
limitations: Lack of detailed analysis on the impact of teacher quality variance on student performance.
No reported experiments scaling MOPD beyond three domains to assess scalability limits.
Limited discussion on computational cost and latency trade-offs in large-scale deployments.
Absence of theoretical guarantees or formal convergence analysis for the distillation process.
open_questions: How does MOPD scale with an increasing number of domain teachers and more heterogeneous capabilities?
What are the effects of teacher model quality and domain overlap on the final student performance?
Can MOPD be extended to incorporate dynamic teacher updates or online teacher-student co-training?
How does the choice between policy-gradient and top-k loss variants affect convergence speed and final model robustness?

papers.title: IHDec: Divergence-Steered Contrastive Decoding for Securing Multi-Turn Instruction Hierarchies
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail to maintain instruction hierarchies (IH) when processing multi-source inputs with varying role-level priorities, paradoxically adhering to lower-priority directives during conflicts. While existing defenses mitigate this issue, they are largely restricted to single-turn scenarios and require expensive fine-tuning. In this paper, we formalize this failure mode in multi-turn contexts via a Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) framework, uncovering a pervasive role-influence inversion phenomenon where subordinate inputs override superior roles. To rectify this without training, we propose IHDec (Instruction Hierarchy-steered Decoding). IHDec leverages JSD to automatically detect token-level hierarchy violations and dynamically executes contrastive decoding to suppress misaligned subordinate roles. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that IHDec outperforms training-based baselines in multi-turn conflicts while fully preserving general response quality. Furthermore, IHDec strengthens safety against adversarial prompt injections and exhibits a robust scaling synergy with larger models. The Code is available at https://github.com/nxcolelxu/IHDec.git

summary.evidence: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that IHDec outperforms training-based baselines in multi-turn conflicts while fully preserving general response quality.
